approach: Differentiate x twice for velocity and acceleration, then find the velocity when x itself is zero.

steps.text: Differentiate x with respect to time to get the velocity, using the chain rule.
Differentiate v with respect to time to get the acceleration.
Substitute t = 2 s into x, v and a.
Set x = 0 to find when the particle is at the origin, then find the velocity there.

final_answer.value: (a) x = 1 m, v = 4 m/s, a = 8 m/s²; (b) velocity at origin = 0 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Differentiating (2t−3)² without the chain-rule factor of 2 from the inner 2t gives v = 2(2t−3), which is 2 m/s at t = 2 s instead of 4 m/s.
Reading 'at origin' as t = 0 instead of x = 0 gives a velocity of −12 m/s instead of 0 m/s.
